body_markdown:
If you haven’t heard, the new BMW 3 Series is available in two versions: one gas and one electric. What unites them is the bold Neue Klasse design, the innovative but controversial ergonomics, and, shall we say, *confident* pricing. Driving the electric BMW i3 50 xDrive and the straight-six–powered M350 xDrive reveals an unexpectedly diverse set of strengths, weaknesses, and emotional feedback. Hop in, buckle up and enjoy the ride!


How’s this for sticker shock: $74,800 for a 3 Series. True, the fire-red M350 (codename G50) was fully loaded, but less than ten grand more would buy you the brawny 503-horsepower M3 Competition. Or how about the $75,500 550e xDrive hybrid, which offers more space, grace, pace, and prestige than the 3?


BMW/Bernhard Filser


BMW/Bernhard Filser


BMW/Bernhard Filser


At $71,400, the i3 50 xDrive (chassis code NA0) we tested was not exactly a bargain, either, and this particular specimen even lacked pricey options like partial leather trim, the desirable adaptive M suspension, fancy 21-inch wheels, and a matte paint finish. Without extras, prices start at $61,500 for the EV and at $65,900 for the M Performance model. At the bottom of the list, we find the 255-hp 330 sedan, which costs $49,900 before options. Due early next year and still to be priced are the 374-hp i3 40 and the go-faster i3 M60, which boasts a feisty 612-hp power pack. There are also two M3s in the works—one[a fully electric four-motor crackerjack](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/check-out-the-pre-production-electric-bmw-m3/) and the other a thorough evolution of the current six-pot car.


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


Like its big brother, the iX3 SUV, the i3 contains BMW’s advanced Neue Klasse tech stack: an 800-volt architecture, a high-end battery rated at 108.7 kWh net, and a maximum charging performance of 400kW for a 21-minute energy boost from 10% to 80%. When all key parameters click, a ten-minute pit stop will bunker 264 more miles of traveling distance. According to the European WLTP cycle, the maximum range is 468 miles. EPA numbers (usually less optimistic) have yet to be finalized.


## Specs: M350 xDrive / i3 50 xDrive


• **Price (base/as tested):** $65,900/$74,800 (M350) / $61,500/$71,400 (i3 50)
• **Powertrain:** 3.0-liter mild hybrid straight-six with 8-speed automatic (M350); two e-motors, single-speed fixed ratio (i3 50)
• **Output:** 437 hp, 428 lb-ft (M350); 463 hp, 476 lb-ft (i3 50)
• **Layout:** Front-engine, four-door, five-passenger AWD sedan (M350); dual e-motor, four-door, five-passenger AWD sedan (i3 50)
• **Weight:** 4169 lb (M350); 5016 lb (i3 50)
• ****0–60 mph** :** 3.9 sec (M350); 4.5 sec (i3 50)
• **EPA fuel economy:** TBD
• **Competitors:** Mercedes-AMG C43; Mercedes-Benz C400 EQ


Fear not, sport sedan fans. The electric i3 is still, first and foremost, a proper BMW and not an anonymous, boring planet saver. We put it to the real test in France’s mountainous Provençal hinterlands, where academic virtues such as the 4.5-second acceleration time from 0 to 60 mph and the 130-mph top speed were totally eclipsed by the massive instant torque, which shoots from the hip with a highly physical 476 lb-ft of forward thrust.


BMW/Bernhard Filser


There are four different recuperation modes to choose from, but they must be accessed via the touchscreen, since shift paddles are conspicuously absent. Which is a shame, because the[upcoming electric M3](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/electric-bmw-im3-will-have-the-voice-of-a-v-10/) has them, and the 3 Series halo car also boasts an intriguing simulated e-shift feature, which will be an essential item for all sporty EVs before long. Also missing in the test car was the highly recommended adaptive M suspension, which spreads the damper calibration over three settings labelled Comfort, Sport, and Sport Plus. Another must-have item are the sports seats, which offer more support for broad shoulders and long thighs as well as a marginally lower driving position. This can be an asset in the i3 50, which is a bit taller than the M350 due to the bulky underfloor energy pack. The batteries kick up the hip point just a touch too much, and they also take away some trunk space, but thanks to the practical frunk the combined total cargo volume equals that of the M350. Since the six-cylinder engine needs a lot more cooling air than the bonsai drivetrain of the i3, the ICE version (Cd 0.28) cannot rival the EV (Cd 0.21) for aerodynamic efficiency.


BMW/Bernhard Filser


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


Panoramic Vision—BMW’s ultra-wide head-up display tech—was first introduced in the iX3. It works better there than in this new 3 Series. How come? It has to do with the different seating position, which can make it hard for tall drivers to see what’s going on behind the upper steering wheel rim. In my case, the effect is best described as Partial Vision, which makes the optional head-up display almost mandatory. Just as irritating is the fact that the driver’s right hand almost constantly obscures the left edge of the parallelogram-shaped center touchscreen, where recurrently used icons like the speed limit and lane departure warnings squat. Magic digits are not only required to access the busy main display but also to operate the transparent smear- and reflection-prone fingertip controls splashed onto the grotesquely over-styled and multi-talented steering wheel. While we greatly appreciate the improved voice command system, could we please get back, ASAP, physical controls for the few remaining air vents, as well as a few knobs and switches for on/off, hot/cold, and volume up/down functions? Last but not least, what good is a panoramic roof that won’t open and doesn’t even have a blind to keep out direct sunlight on a hot day?


BMW/Bernhard Filser


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


Unlike the new Mercedes C-Class, the 2027 BMW 3 Series is not available with rear-wheel steering or air suspension, but the adaptive shock absorbers make a big difference on bumpy and billowy tarmac. Despite the low center of gravity and the nicely balanced weight distribution, the i3 tips the scales at a hefty 5026 pounds, and it shows. Brake dive and acceleration squat are more pronounced than in the M350, and so are roll, pitch, and yaw. The car remains well planted even at speed, but the steering snaps at potholes and transverse undulations, and around the straight-ahead position the helm felt restless on a basic French autoroute.


BMW/Bernhard Filser


In contrast, the 437-hp combustion M350 version was less nervous, better-handling, and more sure-footed overall. The fact that it is 760 pounds lighter obviously helps, and so does that adaptive M suspension. At 3.9 seconds 0–60 mph, the M350 is not only six tenths quicker off the mark than the 463-hp i3, it even beats today’s 473-hp M3 by the blink of an eye. More importantly, these four fat tailpipes play a much more emotional tune than the[synthetic HypersonX](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bmw-hypersonx-soundscape-neue-klasse/) soundtrack composed for the Neue Klasse.


BMW/Bernhard Filser


Make no mistake: The M350 is worth every single drop of high-octane juice it burns. And that’s without us pulling out all the stops; we didn’t have the chance to engage Drift Moment, which disconnects front-wheel drive and sends the full torque load to the rear wheels, where it is masterminded by an electronically controlled mechanical diff. Such a feature used to be reserved for full-blooded M cars, but it may soon also be unlocked for the electric i3 M60.


Whereas the M350 is fitted with four-piston fixed-caliper brakes up front, the eagerly regenerating i3 makes do with single-piston sliding calipers. Oddly enough, the EV nonetheless decelerates even more promptly and with relentless vigor. In contrast, the gas-fed 3 Series is somewhat handicapped by its stopping apparatuses, which feel a tad blunt and heavy when hot.


BMW i3 50 xDrive


BMW/Wolfgang Groeger-Meier


In essence, despite a few missteps, both new 3 Series models comply with the brand’s “Ultimate Driving Machine” slogan. They don’t look all that special inside or out, and the radical reduce-to-the-max ergonomics take some getting used to, but the M350 in particular is spot-on as far as old-school driving feel: delightfully playful and about as quick as a 24/7 daily driver needs to be. While the electric i3 is not quite as much fun, it certainly did its EV homework in terms of consumption, range, and charging time. Value for money might be an issue for both models, but with the all-new gas-powered Mercedes C-Class and the overdue next Audi A4 still nowhere in sight, BMW has the prestigious compact luxury sedan playground all to itself for the time being.


## 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and M350 xDrive


**Highs:** The sweet-handling and beefed up M350 is putty in the hands of a keen driver. The i3 50 jumps to a top spot in the range and efficiency sweepstakes.
**Lows:** Both cars are expensive, even relatively speaking. The ergonomics are not exactly love at first sight. The new cabin’s minimalism doesn’t make it feel particularly premium anymore. **Takeaway:** As a daily driver, the nicely balanced M350 gives the M3 a hard run for the money. In the case of the i3, we would probably try to stretch the budget to the M60 out next spring.
